mappings.note: Dating the US Civil Rights Movement. This item (and the 29 that follow it) is from the DEMOCRACY AND DIVERSITY chapter, misfiled here; the 2-LO frame of this chapter covers only gender/religion/caste in Indian politics and women's representation, so neither LO can be cited. Competency-level recall is the honest level.
Names Martin Luther King Jr as the Civil Rights Movement's leader: factual recall from a chapter whose outcomes are absent from this frame, so C-3.1 rather than a forced LO-1.
Date of the Black Power movement's emergence. Recall of a case fact; LO-1 is confined to India and LO-2 to women's representation.

Asks what social differences are mostly based on (birth, sometimes choice). Defect: the demonstrative 'These' has no antecedent in the loaded stem, so the passage it refers to was lost; the answer is the same either way, which is why it is mapped rather than skipped.
Requires reasoning about WHY a difference becomes a division (overlap with other differences), so the analysis competency C-3.3. Not LO-1, which is restricted to gender, religion and caste in India.
Compares the Northern Ireland and Netherlands social divisions: analysis of democratic practice, C-3.3. No LO in this frame covers either country.
Germany and Sweden were once highly homogeneous: recall of the concept 'homogeneous society' applied to a case. Not C-3.3, since nothing is analysed or evaluated.
Asks for the relation between the politics of social division and democracy, which is an evaluation of democratic practice, C-3.3. Neither LO reaches it.
Catholic-to-Protestant ratio in Northern Ireland: demographic recall, below C-3.3's analytic level.
The UK is predominantly Protestant: recall of the case's religious composition.
The Republic of Ireland is predominantly Catholic: the complement of qid:105475, same recall level.
Date of the 1998 peace agreement in Northern Ireland: chronological recall, not analysis.
Asks how people must perceive their identities (multiple and complementary) for social divisions to be accommodated: the analytic condition, so C-3.3 rather than plain recall.
How leaders should raise community demands (within the constitutional framework, not at another community's cost): an evaluation of democratic practice, C-3.3.
The marginalised fight injustice by the democratic/constitutional path: judgement about democratic practice, C-3.3, not the factual recall of C-3.1.
Identifies the false claim about how democracy deals with social divisions: evaluation of democratic practice, C-3.3.
Three-statement item on overlapping differences, multiple identities and where divisions occur: analysis, C-3.3, not recall.
Sequencing four claims about social divisions and party appeals requires reasoning about cause and consequence, so C-3.3.
Names Yugoslavia as the state that disintegrated over religious and ethnic identity: recall of a case, so C-3.1 rather than C-3.3.

Selects the elements that show India's basic unity: a judgement about which features hold a diverse democracy together, C-3.3. Not LO-1, which asks specifically how gender, religion and caste shape politics.
Peter Norman's gesture at the Mexico Olympics: recall of a case detail.
Defines a homogeneous society. Conceptual recall; no LO covers it.
Meaning of the term African-American: terminology recall.
'Democracy involves ...' tests the concept of democracy itself (competition and accommodation). Generic conceptual recall, so C-3.1; no LO in this two-LO frame applies.
Names the three countries used as social-division cases: recall of the chapter's examples.
Four statements turning on whether class and religion overlap or cut across in Northern Ireland and the Netherlands: the analytic core of the diversity chapter, C-3.3.
Evaluates four claims about what determines the outcome of the politics of social divisions: analysis, C-3.3, not recall.
Identifies the incorrect claim about social division, which requires reasoning about the concept rather than recalling it.
What overlapping differences signify (deeper, more dangerous divisions): the causal claim, C-3.3.
Asks the origin of social differences (birth and choice): definitional recall, so C-3.1 rather than the analytic C-3.3 used for the overlap items.
India has no official state religion: the constitutional relation between religion and the state, which is the religion limb of LO-1. Not LO-2, which is about women.
Defines patriarchy. LO-1 requires the candidate to ANALYSE how gender shapes politics; this item only asks for the term, so the recall competency is cited.
Names family laws. Terminology recall; LO-1 would need the political or communal significance of personal law to be at issue.

Identifies a state with an official religion, which is the religion-and-state relation LO-1 covers, contrasted with Indian secularism. Not C-3.1: the item turns on the political status of religion, not on a term.

One-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities reserved for women is the concrete measure LO-2 evaluates. Not LO-1, since the item is about representation rather than how gender shapes political competition.
Tests what Indian secularism does and does not mean: the religion limb of LO-1. Not C-3.1, because the item requires the candidate to discriminate among claims, not recall a definition.
Defines caste hierarchy. LO-1 concerns caste's effect on politics; this item asks only for the meaning of the social ranking.
The ideas underlying communal politics (that religion is the principal basis of community and that one religion's interests are supreme) is religion influencing politics, LO-1.
Attributes to Gandhi the claim that religion cannot be separated from politics: the religion-and-politics relation, LO-1, not a bare definition.
Defines a secular person. Vocabulary recall; LO-1 would need secularism's political working to be in question, as in qid:105501.
Female literacy rate in India: a statistic. Not LO-2, which is about political representation, and not LO-1, which asks for analysis; this is indicator recall.
The Scandinavian comparison is the chapter's evidence that women's participation in public life can be much higher, which is the argument LO-2 evaluates.
Identifies caste as the division peculiar to India, the caste limb of LO-1. Not C-3.1: the point of the item is caste's place in Indian public life, not its definition.
Characteristics of a patriarchal society: understanding of the concept, as with qid:105497, rather than LO-1's analysis of politics.
Causes of communalism: how religion enters and distorts politics, LO-1. Not C-3.1, since causes must be weighed rather than recalled.
Asks who counts as a feminist: definitional. LO-2 would need the case for women's political representation to be at issue.
Same definition of 'feminist' as qid:105511, worded as a completion. Duplicate target, same code.
Duplicate stem of qid:105507; the high-participation comparison used to argue for greater representation, LO-2.
Requires the candidate to pick the statement that captures Gandhi's position on religion and politics, i.e. religion's legitimate and illegitimate roles in politics, LO-1.
Communalism as a division based on religion: the bare definition, so C-3.1. Contrast qid:105503 and qid:105536, which ask how it operates in politics and therefore take LO-1.

The aims of feminist movements (political and legal equality, better educational and career opportunities) are the demands LO-2 weighs. Not LO-1, which is about how gender shapes political competition.
Meaning of 'feminist': third duplicate of the definition, same recall level as qid:105511.
Negative form of the participation comparison: identifies where women's public participation remains low, the deficit LO-2 evaluates.
Meaning of 'gender division' (a social, not a natural, division based on the sexual division of labour). Definitional; LO-1 asks for its political effect.
Women's share of state assembly seats is the representation statistic LO-2 is built on. Not C-3.1: the figure exists in the chapter precisely to support the case for reservation.

The result of the political expression of gender division is an improved role for women in public life, i.e. representation, LO-2. LO-1 would fit an item asking how gender division enters politics in the first place.
Identifies what is NOT an aim of the feminist movement, so it tests the same set of political demands as qid:105516, LO-2.
The one-third reservation in panchayats and municipalities as the step taken for women's representation: LO-2's central measure.
Indian society described as patriarchal: recall of the characterisation. Not LO-1, which requires analysis of political consequences.

Asks what Gandhi MEANT, i.e. the interpretation that religion means moral values in politics rather than any one faith's supremacy: LO-1's religion-and-politics analysis, a step beyond the attribution item qid:105504.
Which work men spend less time on: the sexual division of labour. Understanding of the concept, not LO-1's political analysis.
Lowest child sex ratio figure: statistical recall, like the literacy item qid:105506.
Names the Equal Remuneration Act. Statute recall, so the institution-recall competency; LO-1 would need the law's political genesis or effect to be analysed.
The blank is 'socio-economic': what changed the caste system. Understanding of the caste system's transformation, not its effect on politics (LO-1).
The ugliest form of communalism (communal violence and riots) is the political consequence of religion-based mobilisation, LO-1, not the bare definition of qid:105515.
The feminist claim that women's well-being is best served by more women in positions of power is exactly the proposition LO-2 asks the candidate to evaluate.
The ceiling on women's share of Lok Sabha seats: the under-representation figure LO-2 rests on, as with qid:105520.
Which matters fall under family law: recall of the subject matter, as with qid:105498.
What is breaking down caste hierarchy (urbanisation, literacy, occupational mobility): socio-economic causes, so understanding of the caste system rather than LO-1's analysis of caste in politics.
The forms communalism takes IN POLITICS (communal appeals, religious mobilisation, communal violence) is LO-1's religion limb stated explicitly.
Meaning of 'communal politics' specifically, i.e. religion used as the basis of political community, LO-1. Contrast qid:105515, which asks only what communalism divides people by.
